title: Topological morphism properties are invariant under arbitrary algebraic-space thickenings
statement: Algebraic spaces and their morphisms are as in [def-trf-algebraic-space], in the universes of [def-weil-size-convention]; their fibre products are [lem-trf-space-fibre-products-etale-covers]. The topology on an algebraic space is the quotient topology from a surjective etale scheme atlas. For a morphism of algebraic spaces, quasi-compact means that inverse images of quasi-compact opens are quasi-compact; quasi-separated means that the diagonal is quasi-compact; separated means that the diagonal is a closed immersion; universally closed means that every algebraic-space base change is closed on underlying topological spaces. Proper means separated, quasi-compact, locally of finite type on etale scheme charts, and universally closed (the scheme convention is [def-weil-finite-type-morphism, def-weil-proper-morphism]). Let $i:X\hookrightarrow X\prime$ and $j:Y\hookrightarrow Y\prime$ be thickenings of algebraic spaces over a scheme $B$ [def-pc-scheme]; here a thickening is a closed immersion inducing a homeomorphism of underlying spaces, and a closed immersion of algebraic spaces is a representable morphism all of whose base changes to schemes are closed immersions of schemes [def-weil-closed-immersion]. Let $f:X\to Y$ and $f\prime:X\prime\to Y\prime$ satisfy $f\prime i=jf$. For each property $\mathcal P$ in the list quasi-compact, quasi-separated, separated, universally closed, one has $$f\text{ has }\mathcal P\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad f\prime\text{ has }\mathcal P.$$ The square need not be cartesian; neither thickening is required to have finite order. No local finite type or flatness hypothesis is imposed.

proof.text: Quasi-compactness: the commutative square identifies the topological map $|f|$ with $|f\prime|$ by the homeomorphisms $|i|$ and $|j|$. For every quasi-compact open $V\prime\subseteq|Y\prime|$, its inverse image $V$ under $|j|$ is a quasi-compact open and $|i|$ restricts to a homeomorphism $f^{-1}(V)\simeq(f\prime)^{-1}(V\prime)$. Every quasi-compact open in $|Y|$ occurs this way. Compactness is preserved in both directions by a homeomorphism: transfer any open cover along the inverse homeomorphism and transfer a finite subcover back. This proves the quasi-compactness equivalence.

Universal closedness, forward direction: assume $f$ universally closed and take any $t:T\prime\to Y\prime$. The fibre-product node supplies $T=Y\times_{Y\prime}T\prime$, $W=X\times_YT$ and $W\prime=X\prime\times_{Y\prime}T\prime$. The thickening base-change node makes $j$ a monomorphism and $T\to T\prime$ a universal homeomorphism. On any test object $H$, a map to $W$ is a triple $(x,y,u)$ satisfying $f(x)=y$ and $j(y)=t(u)$. Forgetting $y$ gives the pair $(x,u)$ with $jf(x)=t(u)$; its inverse sets $y=f(x)$. These mutually inverse descriptions identify $W=X\times_{Y\prime}T\prime=X\times_{X\prime}W\prime$ compatibly with projections. Thus $W\to W\prime$ is a base change of $i$, so it induces a homeomorphism. Write $h:|W|\to|W\prime|$, $b:|T|\to|T\prime|$ for these homeomorphisms, and $p:|W|\to|T|$, $q:|W\prime|\to|T\prime|$ for the projections. Their projections give $qh=bp$. For every closed $C\subseteq|W\prime|$, one has $q(C)=b(p(h^{-1}(C)))$. This set is closed: $h^{-1}(C)$ is closed, $p$ is closed as a base change of $f$, and $b$ is a homeomorphism. Thus every such $q$ is closed, proving universal closedness of $f\prime$.

Universal closedness, reverse direction: assume $f\prime$ universally closed and take $t:T\to Y$, also regarded as a map $jt:T\to Y\prime$. The fibre-product node supplies $W=X\times_YT$ and $V=X\prime\times_{Y\prime}T$. A map from any test object to $X\times_{Y\prime}T$ is a pair $(x,u)$ with $jf(x)=jt(u)$. The monomorphism assertion of the thickening base-change node cancels $j$, giving exactly $f(x)=t(u)$. Therefore $W=X\times_{Y\prime}T=X\times_{X\prime}V$ compatibly with projections. The same node makes $W\to V$ a universal homeomorphism since it is a base change of $i$. Write $h:|W|\to|V|$ for this homeomorphism, $r:|V|\to|T|$ for the projection and $p:|W|\to|T|$ for the required base change of $f$. Compatibility of projections gives $p=rh$. For any closed $C\subseteq|W|$, its image $h(C)$ is closed and $p(C)=r(h(C))$ is closed because $r$ is a base change of $f\prime$. Thus $f$ is universally closed. Steps 1--3 apply to every commutative square whose vertical maps are monomorphisms inducing homeomorphisms after every base change: no further closed-immersion property entered the comparisons. In particular these arguments will apply to the diagonal square once step 4 verifies these precise hypotheses.

To compare the diagonals, put $D=X\times_YX$ and $D\prime=X\prime\times_{Y\prime}X\prime$; these algebraic-space fibre products exist by the cited fibre-product node. Cancellation of the monomorphism $j$ gives $D=X\times_{Y\prime}X$. The comparison $k:D\to D\prime$ factors as $X\times_{Y\prime}X\to X\times_{Y\prime}X\prime\to X\prime\times_{Y\prime}X\prime$. Each arrow is a base change of $i$, so the thickening base-change node makes each a monomorphism inducing a homeomorphism after every base change. The composite $k$ is a monomorphism: equality after $k$ cancels the second arrow and then the first. For any $A\to D\prime$, the base change of $k$ factors through $(X\times_{Y\prime}X\prime)\times_{D\prime}A$. The first factor is a base change of the first displayed arrow and the second of the second displayed arrow, by the fibre-product universal property. Both induce homeomorphisms, so their composite does too. The square with horizontal arrows $\Delta_f,\Delta_{f\prime}$ and vertical arrows $i,k$ commutes, as is seen by its two projections.

Apply the arguments of steps 1--3 to this diagonal square: step 4 supplies precisely the monomorphism and universal-homeomorphism hypotheses those arguments use. Thus $\Delta_f$ is quasi-compact if and only if $\Delta_{f\prime}$ is quasi-compact, which is the quasi-separatedness equivalence by definition. They are also universally closed simultaneously. The separated-diagonal criterion applies to each of the arbitrary morphisms $f,f\prime$ and identifies universal closedness of these diagonals with their being closed immersions. This proves the separatedness equivalence. Together with steps 1--3 it proves all four assertions, without finite order, flatness, or local finite type hypotheses.

lean.statement: theorem thickening_topological_properties_iff {B : Scheme.{u}} {X X' Y Y' : AlgebraicSpace B} (i : X ⟶ X') (j : Y ⟶ Y') (f : X ⟶ Y) (f' : X' ⟶ Y') (hi : IsRepresentableWith (fun _ _ p ↦ IsClosedImmersion p.left) i.hom.hom) (hj : IsRepresentableWith (fun _ _ p ↦ IsClosedImmersion p.left) j.hom.hom) (hi_top : IsHomeomorph (mapPoint i.hom.hom)) (hj_top : IsHomeomorph (mapPoint j.hom.hom)) (hcomm : i ≫ f' = f ≫ j) : ((∀ V : Set (Point Y.obj.obj), IsOpen V → IsCompact V → IsCompact (mapPoint f.hom.hom ⁻¹' V)) ↔ (∀ V : Set (Point Y'.obj.obj), IsOpen V → IsCompact V → IsCompact (mapPoint f'.hom.hom ⁻¹' V))) ∧ ((∀ V : Set (Point (Limits.pullback f.hom.hom f.hom.hom)), IsOpen V → IsCompact V → IsCompact (mapPoint (Limits.pullback.diagonal f.hom.hom) ⁻¹' V)) ↔ (∀ V : Set (Point (Limits.pullback f'.hom.hom f'.hom.hom)), IsOpen V → IsCompact V → IsCompact (mapPoint (Limits.pullback.diagonal f'.hom.hom) ⁻¹' V))) ∧ (MapIsSeparated f ↔ MapIsSeparated f') ∧ (MapIsUniversallyClosed f ↔ MapIsUniversallyClosed f')
lean.note: The first two clauses expand exactly the compact-open preimage conditions stated by this node, including on the presheaf diagonal; they do not silently replace this node’s topological convention by the affine scheme-base-change predicate MapIsQuasiCompact. The other two clauses reuse MapIsSeparated and MapIsUniversallyClosed. Thickenings expand the existing representable closed-immersion test and IsHomeomorph of the canonical mapPoint.
